The investigation workflow is running in the background. Five agents are working in parallel:

  • Compile time and caching: timed clean and warm builds, pinned to 4 cores to match a GitHub runner.
  • pytest: a profile of the slowest tests, plus trials with pytest-xdist and with a release build.
  • Native wheels: whether abi3 is feasible, building several Python versions in one job, macOS cross-compiling, sccache.
  • Job graph: the critical path, duplicated work, and which lanes have caught real failures.
  • GitHub platform facts: runner concurrency limits, cache scoping and Rosetta availability, with sources.

A synthesizer then turns all of that into a ranked plan. All builds run in three throwaway worktrees under treams-ci-*. I'm not touching your checkout and not making any GitHub changes. I'll report when it finishes.

The first investigation is done. A second workflow is now drafting the changes on a local branch ci/speed-up, which is not pushed. Four adversarial reviewers will then check it for lost thoroughness, correctness, speed claims and missed levers.

Where the time actually goes (measured, from 5 runs, median about 18 min)

  • macOS sets the wall-clock in 5 of 5 runs, not the Python lane. There are 8 macOS wheel jobs, but GitHub caps an account at 5 concurrent macOS jobs on any plan. So 3 jobs wait 4–9 min every run. On top of that, Intel macOS builds take 7–13 min.
  • The Python 3.12 lane comes second at about 14.5 min, because it runs four things one after another: build, just check, pytest with coverage, then a second release build in just check-wheel.
  • Nothing caches Rust builds. Every lane compiles from scratch, and about 47% of a clean build is your own crates, which no cache can skip.
  • Some ideas don't pay off:
    • Building several Python versions in one macOS job costs 55% of a clean build per extra interpreter, so it is slower overall.
    • pytest itself isn't the problem: debug-profile code isn't the bottleneck, and imports and collection are cheap.

Change Thoroughness Effect on wall-clock
Split the 3.12 lane into coverage, repo checks and host wheel jobs slightly better (static-check failures no longer hide the test results) needed so the macOS gain counts
Rust dependency cache on macOS wheel jobs (CI only; release builds stay uncached) unchanged together with the split, about 18 → 13–14 min once main has a warm cache
Build Intel macOS wheels on Apple silicon, keep the smoke test on real Intel unchanged for checks, but changes how release wheels are built about another 1.5 min warm, 3–4 min cold
pytest-xdist (needs a small conftest.py fix, or the Rayon guard is silently skipped) unchanged (same 6637 tests and outcomes, identical coverage XML) 8.5 → 6.5 min per lane, but no wall-clock gain until macOS gets shorter

Your CI takes a median of about 19 min (5 clean runs, 15.5–21.5 min). The bottleneck is macOS, not the Python lanes. The branch below should bring it to about 12–13.5 min once a Rust cache exists with no loss of thoroughness, or to about 9–11 min if you accept one small tradeoff. Those projections are simulated from measured job times; nothing has run on GitHub runners yet.

Why it's slow

  • macOS sets the end time in all 5 runs. There are 8 macOS wheel jobs, but GitHub allows only 5 macOS jobs at once per account on every plan. So 3 jobs wait 4–9 min each run, and the Intel builds then take another 6.5–17 min.
  • The Python 3.12 lane runs everything one after another: build, just check, pytest with coverage, then a second release build in just check-wheel. On slow runners it ties the macOS tier.
  • There is no Rust build cache anywhere. Even with one, roughly 2/3 of each macOS release build can't be cached: your own two crates rebuild one after the other with codegen-units=1 plus LTO.

Branch ci/speed-up (local only, not pushed; 5 commits on main, one per change)

Commit What Thoroughness Wall-clock
b1ddecb Split the 3.12 lane into coverage, a Repository checks job and a Host release wheel job slightly better: static-check failures no longer stop the tests from running (this happened in one past run) only counts together with the cache
bf480df Drop Rust debug info in CI dev builds (debug assertions and overflow checks stay on) unchanged none; about 11 runner-min saved per run
9290e31 Rust dependency cache on the macOS wheel jobs; release builds skip it unchanged the main gain, once warm
25592d5 pytest-xdist, plus a conftest.py fix unchanged: same 6641 tests and outcomes, identical coverage about 2x per test lane; failures show 1.5–3 min sooner
9ebfdea Draft: build the Intel macOS wheels on Apple silicon, smoke-test them on real Intel runners unchanged for checks, but changes how released Intel wheels are built about 1–1.5 min warm, about 3 min cold

The conftest.py fix matters: without it, xdist silently skips your Rayon global-pool check. There is now a test that fails if that ever happens.

Projected median run times

  • Whole branch, warm cache: about 12–13.5 min. On a cold cache it's about 15.5–16.5 min; the first push to a PR is cold until main has saved a cache.
  • Dropping the Intel cross-build commit: about 13.5–14 min warm.
  • The bigger lever (not implemented, your call): use codegen-units=16 only for macOS wheels built on PRs and pushes, and drop the Intel cross-build commit. That gives about 9–11 min warm, and the release-path workflow stays untouched.
    • The tradeoff: CI-built macOS wheels wouldn't use the exact codegen setting you ship. Every PR still builds the real release profile on Linux, and release candidates rebuild and smoke-test all 20 wheels from scratch.
    • In practice, a macOS-only problem specific to codegen-units=1 would show up at release time instead of on the PR.
    • It's one line of YAML.

Settings that need no code

  • Cache retention: raise it in Settings → Actions → Caches. The default is 7 days, and main had idle gaps of 7 and 8 days last month, so those first PRs would start cold. This beats a scheduled warm-up job.
  • macOS cap: you can ask GitHub Support to raise the 5-job limit. Their docs say they can, but I don't know if they will for a personal account.

Rejected, and why

  • Several Python versions per macOS job: each extra interpreter costs 55% of a full build, so it's slower.
  • Building wheels only on main: run 37117567002 had a compile error only the Windows wheel jobs caught, and merge queues aren't available for personal accounts.
  • paths-ignore: it would leave the required check pending.
  • Testing against release builds: it loses debug assertions.
  • abi3 wheels (5 builds instead of 20): they work technically. After the other changes they'd save only about 1.5–2 min more, at the cost of changing the shipped wheels.

Verified locally

  • actionlint with shellcheck passes at every commit.
  • just check-static, just docs-check, the workflow and release tests, and the host-wheel job in its minimal environment all pass.
  • The full suite gives the same 6619 passed and 22 skipped serially (97 s) and with xdist (42 s) on 4 cores. Three more xdist runs on a 2-core-plus-SMT setup like a GitHub runner were green.

Not verified: anything on GitHub runners. That includes the real cache restore/save times, xdist on 3.13–3.15 and the NumPy and lower-bounds lanes, and all of the Intel cross-build draft (wheel tag, YAML anchors, the build itself).
